passage:
Monday, deep winter. Sabina, thirteen months, wears three sweaters and can barely bend. She pulls herself up on the charpai, wobbles, and sits down hard. Himani, her mother, laughs and peels one sweater off.
Thursday, in the sunny courtyard. Sabina lets go of the charpai and takes two stiff steps towards the Lohri bonfire pile before plopping down.
The next Sunday. She walks five steps to her Dadi's lap, arms out, grinning, woollen socks slipping.

qa.q: How many sweaters was Sabina wearing on Monday?
qa.a: Three sweaters.

qa.q: What does Sabina's grin as she walks to Dadi suggest?
qa.a: Sabina seems delighted and proud, excited to reach Dadi on her own feet.

qa.q: How did Himani help Sabina's walking in the cold?
qa.a: By taking off a sweater so Sabina could bend and move more freely, and letting her practise in the sunny courtyard.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel as Sabina walks to her lap?
qa.a: Dadi would likely feel joyful and proud, watching real steps come towards her.

grounding: Over a winter week around Lohri, a toddler moves from wobbling at the charpai to walking five steps.

passage: It had rained for four days straight in their Mumbai flat, and Sunaina, two, was bored of the floor. She dragged the plastic stool to the sofa, climbed onto it, then onto the cushions, then stood up, wobbling, arms raised. "Big!" Her Nani, Alka, caught her breath but didn't grab her. She moved the stool away and piled pillows on the floor. Sunaina climbed down backwards, feet first, the way Nani showed her, and then climbed straight back up.

qa.q: What did Sunaina drag to the sofa?
qa.a: The plastic stool.

qa.q: How was Sunaina feeling when she stood on the cushions and said 'Big!'?
qa.a: Sunaina felt proud and excited at climbing up high on her own.

qa.q: How did Nani keep the climbing safe without stopping it?
qa.a: She moved the stool away, put pillows on the floor, and showed Sunaina how to climb down backwards, feet first.

qa.q: What was it like for Alka when Sunaina stood up on the cushions?
qa.a: Alka felt a jolt of fear but chose to stay calm and make the space safer instead of grabbing her.

grounding: During a long monsoon spell indoors, a toddler practises climbing while her grandmother makes it safe.

passage:
"Chaitu, wait! Diyas!" Eshaan moved the lamps back from the terrace edge.
"Run! Run!" Chaitanya, two and a half, zoomed in circles, arms flapping.
"Okay, run, but here, on the mat side. Ready?"
"Ready!"
"Go to the flowerpot and back!"
Chaitanya ran, stopped short, turned without falling, and raced back into Papa's knees.
"Again!"
"Now jump like a frog."
Chaitanya squatted, bounced, landed on both feet, and shrieked with laughter.

qa.q: Where did Eshaan tell Chaitanya to run?
qa.a: On the mat side, to the flowerpot and back.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's shriek of laughter suggest?
qa.a: Chaitanya was delighted and thrilled, enjoying running and jumping.

qa.q: How did Eshaan support Chaitanya's running safely on Diwali night?
qa.a: He moved the diyas away and gave a clear safe route and simple challenges, like running to the flowerpot and frog jumps.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel when Chaitanya turns without falling?
qa.a: Eshaan would likely feel proud and relieved, seeing his son's growing control.

grounding: On a Diwali terrace, a father channels his toddler's running and jumping into safe games.

passage: Before Dussehra, Tanuja sat in the courtyard of their village house threading marigold garlands. Mridul, fifteen months, sat beside the heap of flowers. He pinched one orange marigold between finger and thumb, stared at it, and dropped it into her brass plate. Plop. He did it again, tongue poking out. Tanuja nudged the plate a little further away. Mridul shuffled, pinched, reached, plopped, and clapped his hands.

qa.q: Where did Mridul drop the flowers?
qa.a: Into her brass plate.

qa.q: What does Mridul's tongue poking out suggest?
qa.a: Mridul was concentrating hard, absorbed and pleased with the game.

qa.q: How did Tanuja make the task a little harder in a good way?
qa.a: She nudged the plate further away, so Mridul had to reach, pinch and aim, building finger control.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel watching him?
qa.a: Tanuja probably feels amused and proud, seeing him practise such a careful grasp while she works.

grounding: In a village courtyard before Dussehra, a toddler practises pinching and placing marigolds.

passage: On Christmas Eve in Uppsala, the kitchen smelled of rice porridge and cinnamon. Santiago, twenty months, refused to be fed. "Me!" He gripped the spoon in his fist, scooped, tipped half onto the table, and got the rest into his mouth. His mother, Ingrid, didn't wipe anything. She gently turned his wrist so the spoon stayed flat. On the next scoop, most of it arrived. Santiago banged the spoon on the bowl, beaming, porridge on his nose.

qa.q: What did the kitchen smell of on Christmas Eve?
qa.a: Rice porridge and cinnamon.

qa.q: How did Santiago feel when most of the porridge reached his mouth?
qa.a: Santiago felt proud and happy, banging the spoon and beaming.

qa.q: What small help did Ingrid give, and why was it useful?
qa.a: She turned his wrist so the spoon stayed flat, helping him succeed while still feeding himself.

qa.q: How might Ingrid see the spilled porridge?
qa.a: Ingrid sees the mess as part of learning, not a problem, so she lets Santiago keep trying.

grounding: On Christmas Eve in Sweden, a toddler insists on using a spoon himself and his mother gives a small assist.

passage: I'm Omkar, Charu's big brother. In May it was too hot to go out, so after lunch we stayed under the fan with my wooden blocks. Charu is two. At first she only knocked my towers down. Then one afternoon she put one block on another, holding her breath. Then a third. It fell. She looked at me like she might cry, then picked the block up again. Four stayed up. She clapped so hard she knocked them down herself.

qa.q: When did they play with the blocks?
qa.a: After lunch in May, under the fan.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when the third block fell?
qa.a: Charu seemed upset and close to crying, but determined enough to try again.

qa.q: How could Omkar support Charu's stacking?
qa.a: He could offer big, easy blocks, cheer her tries, and let her build without taking over.

qa.q: How does Omkar see Charu's progress?
qa.a: Omkar watches closely and seems proud, noticing how she went from knocking towers down to stacking four.

grounding: A big brother describes his toddler sister learning to stack blocks during hot summer afternoons.

passage: On Holi morning, the colony courtyard in Jaipur was wet and pink. Arohi, twenty-two months, toddled after the bigger children, her white frock streaked green. Her foot slid on a puddle. She swayed, flung both arms out wide, bent her knees, and stayed up. Her mother, Anjali, one step behind, let out a breath and didn't pick her up. Arohi looked back at her, surprised at herself, then carried on, arms still out like wings.

qa.q: What was the courtyard like on Holi morning?
qa.a: Wet and pink.

qa.q: What did Arohi's look back at her mother suggest?
qa.a: Arohi seemed surprised and a little proud that she hadn't fallen.

qa.q: How did Anjali support Arohi's balance on the slippery courtyard?
qa.a: She stayed one step behind, close enough to help, but let Arohi catch herself instead of picking her up.

qa.q: What was it like for Anjali when Arohi slid?
qa.a: Anjali felt a moment of fear, then relief, choosing to trust Arohi's steadiness.

grounding: On a slippery Holi morning, a toddler catches her balance with arms and knees while her mother stays close.

passage:
"New boots, Uday! For the rain."
Uday, two, stood still, staring at his big yellow gumboots.
"Walk to Mamma?" Shreya crouched at the end of the verandah.
Uday took a heavy step. Clomp. He tipped sideways, grabbed the pillar, steadied himself.
"Hold on. Now let go."
"No."
"Okay. Hold on and walk."
Clomp, clomp. He let go of the pillar himself. Clomp. He wobbled, bent his knees, stayed up.
"Uday! You did it!"
"Again!" He turned, carefully, and clomped back.

qa.q: What colour were Uday's new gumboots?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt when he refused to let go of the pillar?
qa.a: Uday felt unsure and a bit nervous in the heavy new boots.

qa.q: How did Shreya help Uday build confidence in his balance?
qa.a: She accepted his 'no', let him hold on, and waited until he chose to let go himself.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel when Uday lets go by himself?
qa.a: Shreya would likely feel delighted and proud, seeing him gain confidence at his own pace.

grounding: At the start of the monsoon, a toddler learns to balance in heavy new gumboots with his mother's patient encouragement.

passage: Daycare note, the week before Christmas. Karthik (2) spent a long time on the balance beam we set up beside the paper-star decorations. It's only a plank on the floor. At first he walked it sideways, holding the wall. Today he walked it facing forward, arms out, and when he wobbled, he crouched low instead of falling. He did it four times. Next week I'll add a second plank at an angle, and I'll tell his parents. — Vikas

qa.q: What was the balance beam made of?
qa.a: A plank on the floor.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt when he crouched instead of falling?
qa.a: Karthik was probably a little startled but steady, and pleased enough to try four times.

qa.q: What is Vikas planning next, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Adding a second plank at an angle, a slightly harder challenge that builds on his new balance.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents react to the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and happy to hear about his progress, and might try a similar game at home.

grounding: A daycare teacher's pre-Christmas note records a toddler learning to steady himself on a floor plank.

passage: Winter in their village near Mandi meant layers: woollen pyjamas, socks, a thick sweater. Sumit, two, was playing with pine cones on the sunny steps when he suddenly stopped, tugged at the waist of his pyjamas, and wriggled. "Su-su!" he shouted. His mother, Vidya, dropped the washing and ran him to the bathroom. They made it, just. "You told me! Well done." Sumit looked very serious, then went back to his pine cones.

qa.q: What was Sumit playing with?
qa.a: Pine cones on the sunny steps.

qa.q: What does Sumit's serious look afterwards suggest?
qa.a: Sumit seemed proud and a little surprised that telling his mother worked.

qa.q: How could Vidya help Sumit keep noticing this signal in winter?
qa.a: She could dress him in pyjamas that pull down easily and keep praising him for telling her early.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel after they made it in time?
qa.a: Vidya probably felt relieved and pleased, seeing Sumit notice and name the signal.

grounding: On a winter day in a Himachal village, a toddler notices his need for the toilet and tells his mother.

passage: During the June street festival in Lisbon, the whole neighbourhood smelled of grilled sardines, and music played till late. Sofia, two, danced on her mother's feet until almost ten. Then she stopped, rubbed her eyes, and pulled at Beatriz's skirt. "Cama," she said. "Bed." Beatriz knelt. "You're tired?" Sofia nodded and leaned her head on her mother's shoulder. Beatriz carried her home under the paper garlands, and Sofia was asleep before the second corner.

qa.q: What did the neighbourhood smell of?
qa.a: Grilled sardines.

qa.q: How was Sofia feeling when she said 'Cama'?
qa.a: Sofia felt tired and sleepy, and knew she needed to rest.

qa.q: Why was it good that Beatriz asked 'You're tired?'
qa.a: It named the feeling for Sofia, helping her link the body signal to the word.

qa.q: How might Beatriz feel carrying Sofia home?
qa.a: Beatriz probably felt tender and glad that Sofia could tell her she was tired.

grounding: At a summer street festival in Portugal, a toddler notices her tiredness and asks for bed.

passage: I'm Pradeep, Lavanya's uncle. At our Onam lunch, the sadya took forever to be served. Lavanya, not quite two, was fine for the first hour. Then she stopped patting the flower pookalam, came to me, patted her tummy and said, "Mum-mum." She opened her mouth like a little bird. I don't know if she was really hungry or had just seen the payasam. But I gave her a bit of banana from the leaf, and she stopped fussing at once.

qa.q: What did Pradeep give Lavanya from the leaf?
qa.a: A bit of banana.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have been feeling when she patted her tummy?
qa.a: Lavanya was probably hungry and impatient after the long wait.

qa.q: How could adults help Lavanya connect her tummy signal to eating?
qa.a: Respond to her 'mum-mum' quickly and name it, 'You're hungry', so she learns the signal works.

qa.q: How does Pradeep read Lavanya's signal?
qa.a: Pradeep isn't sure whether she was hungry or had just seen the payasam, but responds kindly and notices she settles.

grounding: An uncle describes a toddler signalling hunger during a long Onam lunch.

passage: On Baisakhi morning in their village near Moga, Bebe Baljeet was tying her hair when she said, "Pradeep, bring me my chunni. The yellow one, on the charpai." Pradeep, sixteen months, had no words yet except "ma" and "ba". He looked at the charpai, toddled over, and tugged the yellow cloth until it slid off. He dragged it across the yard to her. "Shabaash!" Bebe laughed. Pradeep beamed and went back for her shoes, which nobody had asked for.

qa.q: What colour was Bebe's chunni?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's beaming show?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud and happy at being praised for bringing the chunni.

qa.q: What could Bebe do to keep building Pradeep's understanding?
qa.a: Give short, clear requests with one or two details, point if needed, and praise him when he follows them.

qa.q: How might Bebe see Pradeep bringing her shoes too?
qa.a: Bebe probably found it funny and sweet, a sign he understands and wants to help.

grounding: On Baisakhi morning, a toddler without words follows his grandmother's two-part instruction.

passage: In Nairobi the long rains had kept everyone indoors for days. When the sun finally broke through one April afternoon, Wanjiru, Aiko's nanny, said, "Aiko, get your boots. We're going outside." Aiko, fourteen months, couldn't say "boots" yet. But she crawled straight to the door, patted her red rain boots, and looked up. "Yes, those!" Wanjiru said. Aiko squealed and held up one foot.

qa.q: What colour were Aiko's rain boots?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: How was Aiko feeling when she squealed and held up her foot?
qa.a: Aiko felt excited and happy about going outside after days indoors.

qa.q: How can Wanjiru keep helping Aiko understand words?
qa.a: Keep naming things clearly and confirming, like 'Yes, those!', whenever Aiko shows she understood.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru feel when Aiko pats the boots?
qa.a: Wanjiru would likely feel pleased and delighted to see Aiko understand the word before she can say it.

grounding: After the long rains in Kenya, a toddler shows she understands 'boots' before she can say it.

passage: I'm Eshaan, Ujjwal's cousin. The week before Diwali, Chachi gave Ujjwal a cleaning job too. He's only eighteen months and says maybe three words. "Ujjwal, put the ball in the box," she said. He picked up the ball, walked to the box and dropped it in. "Now the car." The car went in. "Now give Eshaan Bhaiya a hug." He came and hugged my leg. I'm not sure he knew every word, but he got all three right.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal put in the box first?
qa.a: The ball.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have felt hugging Eshaan's leg?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed happy and affectionate, pleased to be part of the game.

qa.q: Why did Chachi's instructions work well for Ujjwal?
qa.a: They were short, one step at a time, and about familiar objects, so he could follow without speaking.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Ujjwal's understanding?
qa.a: Eshaan is impressed that Ujjwal followed all three, though unsure he knew every word.

grounding: An older cousin watches a nearly wordless toddler follow simple instructions during Diwali cleaning.

passage:
First day of the wedding week. Damini, twenty months, points at the laddoo tray and shouts, "Aaa!" Farhan, her papa, says, "Laddoo? Say laddoo." She just points harder.
Mehendi night. In the crowd, Damini tugs Farhan's kurta and says, "Du. Du!" He hands her one, laughing.
The morning after the wedding. At breakfast she says clearly, "Papa, more laddoo," and every aunty at the table cheers.

qa.q: What does Damini say at breakfast after the wedding?
qa.a: Papa, more laddoo.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she pointed harder at the tray?
qa.a: Damini felt frustrated and impatient, wanting the laddoo but not yet able to say it.

qa.q: How did Farhan help Damini find her words?
qa.a: He named the laddoo and invited her to say it, then answered her attempt 'du' by handing one over.

qa.q: How might the aunties feel when they cheer?
qa.a: The aunties feel delighted and amused, celebrating her new sentence along with the wedding.

grounding: Across a winter wedding week, a toddler moves from pointing and sounds to a short sentence.

passage: During Ganesh Chaturthi, the drums from the pandal shook the windows of their Pune flat. Vishal, two, stood on the sofa, pointing. "Dum dum!" His mother, Disha, picked him up. "Drums. Big drums. Shall we see Ganpati?" "Ganpati see!" They went down to the lane as the idol passed. Vishal waved both hands and shouted, "Bappa! Bye Bappa!" A man nearby laughed and shouted back, "Morya!"

qa.q: What did Vishal call the drums at first?
qa.a: Dum dum.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel as the idol passed?
qa.a: Vishal was excited and joyful, waving both hands and shouting.

qa.q: How did Disha help Vishal's language grow?
qa.a: She repeated his word as the proper one, 'Drums. Big drums', and asked a simple question he could answer.

qa.q: How might the man nearby feel hearing Vishal shout?
qa.a: The man seemed amused and warm, joining in with 'Morya!'

grounding: During Ganesh Chaturthi in Pune, a toddler moves from sound words to short phrases with his mother's help.

passage:
"Mehak, what do you want?" Sarika asked at the kulfi cart. The May heat made everything sticky.
Mehak, two, pointed. "Dat."
"Which one? Mango or pista?"
"Mango."
"Mango kulfi. Say please."
"Pees."
"Good. Here you go."
Mehak licked it and frowned. "Cold!"
"Yes, very cold."
"Mehak cold!" She held out her sticky hand.
"You want me to hold it?"
"Mamma hold." Mehak shook her fingers, then grabbed the kulfi back. "Mehak eat!"

qa.q: Which kulfi did Mehak choose?
qa.a: Mango.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she said 'Cold!' and frowned?
qa.a: Mehak was surprised and a little uncomfortable at how cold the kulfi was.

qa.q: How did Sarika help Mehak use more words?
qa.a: She offered a choice between two flavours, modelled 'please', and repeated Mehak's words back.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel when Mehak grabs the kulfi back?
qa.a: Sarika probably found it funny and sweet, seeing her daughter's growing will and words.

grounding: On a hot May evening, a toddler uses new words and two-word phrases to choose and manage a kulfi.

passage: I'm Ishita, Zainab's neighbour. On Uttarayan everyone flies kites in our Ahmedabad pol. Zainab is one and a half. Her Abbu held her while a red kite dipped behind the water tank. She stared at the tank, not at the sky, waiting. When the kite popped out the other side, she squealed and pointed. It went behind the tank three times. Every time, she was already looking at the right side before it came out.

qa.q: What colour was the kite?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What did Zainab's squeal suggest when the kite reappeared?
qa.a: Zainab felt delighted and excited that the kite came back where she expected.

qa.q: How could Zainab's family play with this new skill?
qa.a: They could play simple hide-and-reappear games, like rolling a ball behind a cushion, and cheer when she looks to the right place.

qa.q: How does Ishita see Zainab's watching?
qa.a: Ishita is impressed and amused, noticing that Zainab looks to the right side before the kite appears.

grounding: On the kite festival, a neighbour sees a toddler track a kite and anticipate where it will reappear.

passage:
First rainy Sunday. Hemant, Ojas's Dadu, set up a toy train on the floor with a cardboard tunnel. Ojas, fourteen months, watched the engine go in and stared at the spot where it vanished.
Next Sunday, still raining. When the engine went in, Ojas's eyes slid ahead to the far end. He crawled there and waited.
The third Sunday. Ojas pointed at the far end before the train even entered, and laughed when it came out right under his finger.

qa.q: What was the tunnel made of?
qa.a: Cardboard.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when the train came out under his finger?
qa.a: Ojas felt delighted and excited, laughing because he had guessed right.

qa.q: How did Dadu's simple game support Ojas's development?
qa.a: Repeating the same train and tunnel each week let Ojas practise following it and predicting where it would come out.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel watching Ojas point before the train entered?
qa.a: Hemant would likely feel proud and pleased, seeing his grandson learn to anticipate.

grounding: Over three rainy Sundays, a toddler learns to anticipate where his grandfather's toy train will emerge.

passage: At the Christmas fair on Park Street, Kalyani bought a bubble wand, and Harsha, sixteen months, sat in his pram under the strings of lights. She blew a big bubble. His eyes followed it up, past the lamp post. When it drifted behind a balloon seller, he leaned sideways, looked to the other side, and caught it again as it came out. Pop. He gasped and slapped the pram. "Ba!" He wanted another.

qa.q: What did Kalyani buy at the fair?
qa.a: A bubble wand.

qa.q: What did Harsha's gasp and slap of the pram show?
qa.a: Harsha felt surprised and delighted when the bubble popped, and eager for another.

qa.q: How could Kalyani keep playing with Harsha's tracking?
qa.a: Blow bubbles slowly in different directions and let him follow and find them, naming them as they go.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel watching him lean to find the bubble?
qa.a: Kalyani would probably feel amused and proud of his sharp eyes.

grounding: At a Christmas fair in Kolkata, a toddler follows a bubble with his eyes and finds it again after it disappears.

passage: On a foggy January morning in their village near Mathura, everyone stayed under the razai. Jatin, eleven months, was playing with a wooden rattle when his mother, Vandana, slid it under the edge of the quilt. Jatin stared at the lump. Then he flung the quilt back with both hands, grabbed the rattle, and shook it triumphantly. Vandana hid it again, deeper. Jatin crawled after it, burrowing and giggling.

qa.q: Where did Vandana hide the rattle?
qa.a: Under the edge of the quilt.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when he found the rattle?
qa.a: Jatin felt triumphant and delighted, shaking it proudly.

qa.q: How did Vandana make the game grow with Jatin?
qa.a: She hid the rattle deeper the second time, a slightly harder search.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel as Jatin burrows and giggles?
qa.a: Vandana probably enjoys it, happy and amused, seeing him understand that the rattle is still there.

grounding: On a foggy winter morning, a baby searches under a quilt for a hidden rattle.

passage: At Lunar New Year in Toronto, Bao hid a red envelope under a cushion while his son Kwame, thirteen months, watched from the rug. Kwame looked at the cushion, then at his father. Bao waited. Kwame crawled over, pushed the cushion with both hands, and grabbed the envelope. He waved it, crackling, and laughed. His grandmother clapped from the sofa. Then Kwame put the envelope back under the cushion himself and looked up: your turn.

qa.q: What did Bao hide under the cushion?
qa.a: A red envelope.

qa.q: What did Kwame's look up after hiding the envelope suggest?
qa.a: Kwame was excited and wanted to keep playing, inviting his father to take a turn.

qa.q: How can Bao build on this game?
qa.a: Hide the envelope under two cushions or a blanket, and let Kwame hide things for him to find too.

qa.q: How might Kwame's grandmother feel clapping from the sofa?
qa.a: She probably feels delighted and proud, enjoying the family game during the festival.

grounding: At Lunar New Year in Canada, a toddler finds an envelope hidden under a cushion and turns it into a game.

passage: I'm Gurleen. In the summer holidays I help the aunty next door with her daughter Uma after lunch. Uma is fourteen months. Yesterday I hid her squeaky duck under my dupatta while she watched. She stared at the dupatta, then pulled it off my lap and squeaked the duck at me. So I hid it behind my back. She crawled round me until she found it. I think she knows now that things don't just vanish.

qa.q: What toy did Gurleen hide?
qa.a: Uma's squeaky duck.

qa.q: What might Uma have felt when she squeaked the duck at Gurleen?
qa.a: Uma seemed pleased and proud of finding it, perhaps even teasing Gurleen with it.

qa.q: How did Gurleen make the game harder, and why is that helpful?
qa.a: Gurleen hid the duck out of sight instead of under the dupatta, which made Uma search around and stretched her understanding.

qa.q: How might Uma's mother feel about Gurleen's help?
qa.a: Uma's mother would likely feel grateful and relieved to have Gurleen playing with Uma on hot afternoons.

grounding: A young neighbour describes a toddler searching for a hidden toy on hot summer afternoons.

passage: When the first monsoon rain hit their village near Bhopal, Rehana, twenty months, was on the verandah. Sumit, the neighbour's boy, ran out into it, stamping. Rehana stared, then held her hand out past the roof. Cold drops. She shrieked and pulled it back, then stuck it out again, laughing. Her Ammi carried her to the edge of a puddle. Rehana stamped once, twice, and splashed Sumit. They both collapsed into giggles.

qa.q: What did Sumit do when the rain started?
qa.a: Ran out into it, stamping.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when she held her hand out in the rain?
qa.a: Rehana felt surprised and then delighted, shrieking and laughing.

qa.q: How did Ammi support Rehana's joy safely?
qa.a: She carried Rehana to the edge of the puddle so she could stamp and splash while staying close.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel being splashed?
qa.a: Sumit seemed to enjoy it, collapsing into giggles and sharing the fun.

grounding: In the first monsoon rain in a village, a toddler shows pure delight at drops and puddles.

passage: In a Seoul park in late October, the ginkgo trees had turned gold. Mina raked a pile of fallen leaves and tossed a handful over her son Paulo, two. He froze, blinked, then burst out laughing. "Again!" She threw more. Paulo spun in circles under the falling leaves, arms up, squealing. Then he grabbed a fistful and threw it at her face. Mina pretended to fall over, and Paulo laughed so hard he sat down.

qa.q: What colour had the ginkgo trees turned?
qa.a: Gold.

qa.q: How was Paulo feeling as he spun under the leaves?
qa.a: Paulo was full of joy and excitement, squealing with his arms up.

qa.q: What made Mina's play so delightful for Paulo?
qa.a: She repeated the surprise, then let him turn the game back on her and played along.

qa.q: How might Mina feel pretending to fall over?
qa.a: Mina probably felt playful and happy, enjoying his laughter.

grounding: In an autumn park in South Korea, a toddler bursts with joy at a leaf-throwing game with his mother.

passage: I'm Tushar, and my little cousin Shalini came to her first garba night this Navratri. She's two. At first she hid behind her mother's chaniya choli, scared of the drums. Then the circle started turning, lights twinkling, and a lady handed her a tiny pair of dandiya sticks. Shalini banged them together. Click. She looked at me, amazed. Click, click. Then she started bouncing, laughing so hard she dropped the sticks. I've never seen her face that bright.

qa.q: What did a lady hand Shalini?
qa.a: A tiny pair of dandiya sticks.

qa.q: How did Shalini's feelings change during the garba night?

"No pram! Out!" Seema, two, kicked at the straps in the crowded Eid market.
"Too many people, jaan. Stay in till the bangle shop."
"OUT!" Seema went red and threw her sipper onto the road.
Sabina picked it up. "You're angry. You want to walk."
"Walk!"
"I know. Hold my finger and push the pram with me?"
"Push?"
"You push. I steer."
Seema gripped the handle, stopped crying, and pushed, very seriously, all the way to the bangles.

qa.a: Seema felt angry and frustrated at being strapped in when she wanted to walk.

passage: Playschool note, first cold week of December. Pankaj (2) struggled at outdoor time again. When I zipped his jacket, he screamed, dropped to the floor and kicked. He stomped outside scowling, then forgot and chased the ball. I'll show his mother the trick. — Baljeet
